summary: Knox County light marking Two-Bush Channel, recommended by the Lighthouse Board in 1892, lit 10 November 1897, automated in 1964.

structures.note: Archive gives 42 ft (12.8 m) from base to the centre of the lantern.

access.note: Not open to the public (archive). Closed during the seabird nesting season, April through August, and the tower is closed (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Lighthouse Board recommends a light and fog signal on the southeast point of Two-Bush Island, at not more than $19,000
$19,000 for the light and fog signal is listed in the Board's appropriations asked for 1894-95; LighthouseFriends gives 18 August 1894 as the appropriation
Title to the island acquired by condemnation; buildings expected that season
Brick tower, fog signal building, dwelling and boathouse built under contract with W. H. Glover Co. of Rockport ($12,250, per LighthouseFriends)
Light and fog signal established 10 November 1897
LighthouseFriends alone reports a fourth-order lens installed in the tower; the archive records only the 1897 fifth-order optic
Red daymark painted white in spring 1914 (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper Leland Mann rescues one man in a motor boat drifting before a northwest wind (13 November). The Bulletin entry gives no year; LighthouseFriends dates the rescue to 1922.
Keeper Leland Mann assists the occupant of a small boat drifting before a northwest wind (2 June, Bulletin 1923)
Remote control from Whitehead; last Coast Guard crew leaves 25 September 1964; station unattended
Keepers' duplex blown up by U.S. Army in a demolition exercise (LighthouseFriends only)
Ownership transferred to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive records a fifth-order lens installed in 1897. LighthouseFriends reports a fourth-order lens installed in the tower in 1902. Both are kept; the 1902 change is not in the archive and is marked as LighthouseFriends' claim.
The archive makes Mann head keeper from 1921; LighthouseFriends makes him head keeper from 1927. The Bulletin calls him keeper in 1922 and 1923, which does not decide the question.

notes_for_editor: The Lighthouse Board's report for fiscal 1892 is printed in 1893 (running head 1893); the Two-Bush passages were checked on the page images: printed p. 44 (scan p. 375) carries the Muscle Ridge passage and printed p. 45 (scan p. 376) the Two-Bush passages and the Whitehead count. The four-month vessel count table is garbled in the OCR, so the story quotes the Board's own words and not the figures; LighthouseFriends gives 6,853 and 3,931 (not used). Sources disagree on the lens: archive (fifth order 1897) and LighthouseFriends (fourth order 1902). The archive's keeper dates for Leland Mann (head keeper from 1921) conflict with LighthouseFriends (head keeper from 1927). The Bulletin calls him keeper in 1922 and 1923, which does not decide the question. The fog signal: the archive record read here (archives.uslhs.org/places/two-bush-island) records a fog signal building built in 1897 and does not mention a horn; an earlier note that it describes a horn came from an unread chart record and is dropped. LighthouseFriends describes a fog bell struck by clockwork, and the story follows it. The 1902 Clara Bella rescue that LighthouseFriends describes (with the dog Smut) is not used: no source found for it, and the 1902 newspaper search returned nothing. The 1970 demolition by Army personnel is LighthouseFriends' claim alone. The Bulletin 1922 entry gives no year; the 1922 date is LighthouseFriends'. The Bulletin 1923 entry is dated 2 June by the Bulletin. The 1897 lighting date is from the Board's own note. The 1914 daymark change and the 1964 and 1998 events are LighthouseFriends' accounts. The 1894 appropriation date (18 August) is LighthouseFriends' and not confirmed in a primary text. The 1893 appropriation figure is read from OCR ('19, 000. 00') and matches the 1892 estimate of 'not exceeding $19,000'. The Wikipedia article was used for leads only. Roster lines carry the archive's person slugs as printed by roster.py; the Coast Guard lines are the archive's 'USCG' heading, with no ranks.
